```json
{
  "winner": "B",
  "reasons": [
    "B is a defined product (a crowdsourced hazard map for urban commuter cyclists) with a named user. A's own source marks its description as 'to confirm' and its customer as 'varies by idea'. A solo operator cannot run a 90-day sales test on a product that is not defined.",
    "B's demand evidence is broader and consistent. At least five independent efforts across nearly a decade (BikeMaps.org, LaneSpotter, Pointz, WABA Crash Tracker, the Davis project) built this same function, and one of them, Pointz, raised $520k. A's demand evidence is a single Reddit post, and a reply in the same thread argues the need is going away because people can 'just vibe code.'",
    "B has a testable non-consumer payer path: advocacy nonprofits that already run hazard-report tools and have dues-paying members, plus municipal or grant funding as shown by BikeMaps.org's $930k grant. None of these is shown to pay a third-party vendor, but each gives a solo founder a short list of organizations to pitch. A's only price anchor, CoFoundersLab at $29/mo, is an adjacent co-founder-matching service, not friend-sourced prototype building.",
    "A's competitive field reads as a commodity trap. The brief lists many near-identical free projects with no traction, two of which show dummy or illustrative data. B's competitors also price at zero, but several have real usage, such as BikeMaps.org active across 9+ cities.",
    "B carries real handicaps. No competitor proves consumers will pay. Pointz needed years and $520k to get to a premium tier. Seeding data density, liability, and moderation are open problems. So B wins on clarity and evidence of need, not on proven willingness to pay."
  ],
  "weakest_evidence_in_loser": "A's demand evidence rests on one Reddit post accessed through a third-party mirror ('Looking for someone to make apps with...'). It is vague about who would pay or what they want built, and a reply in the same thread directly rebuts the premise. A's acquisition cost estimate of $100-200 per customer comes from a vendor blog that the brief itself flags as not independently verified.",
  "confidence_note": "Low-to-moderate confidence. Neither brief shows a validated payer, and both are thin on willingness-to-pay evidence. B is preferred mainly because its concept is defined and its demand signals are corroborated, not because a path to a paying customer within 90 days is demonstrated. If B's nonprofit or municipal buyers will not pay a third party quickly, B could fail the 90-day test as surely as A."
}
```
